title: Piano Trio No. 1 in D minor
hook: The trio Schumann called “the master trio of our time”, opening with a long cello song over a restless piano.

painting.title: View from Reichels Garten over Leipzig in Winter
painting.pairingNote: Mendelssohn was also a gifted watercolourist; he painted this view from his first Leipzig lodgings, in the city where he led the Gewandhaus concerts and gave the trio’s first performance in 1840.

facts: A piano trio is a work for violin, cello and piano. Mendelssohn had planned one for years before he wrote this one in 1839, at thirty, when he was music director of the Gewandhaus concerts in Leipzig. The first movement is dated 6 June and the whole score 18 July 1839.

He kept working on it. After playing it privately with his friend the violinist Ferdinand David in August, he rewrote the whole piece. Then the composer Ferdinand Hiller, a friend of Chopin and Liszt, told him that some of the piano writing, built on broken chords, sounded old-fashioned. Mendelssohn rewrote the piano part again, in a richer and much harder style.
The first public performance was at the Leipzig Gewandhaus on 1 February 1840, with David on violin, Carl Wittmann on cello and Mendelssohn at the piano. Breitkopf & Härtel published it that April.
Robert Schumann reviewed it as “the master trio of our time”, as Beethoven’s and Schubert’s great trios had been in theirs. It is still the most often played of Mendelssohn’s two piano trios.
bigPicture.inOneLine: a passionate song over a storm (I), a song without words (II), a scherzo as light as air (III), and a finale that fights its way from D minor into D major (IV).

movements.heading: Molto allegro agitato
movements.summary: The cello begins with a long, dark song while the piano throbs underneath in restless, off-beat chords. The movement is in [[sonata-form|sonata form]], built from two singing tunes, and the piano keeps up an almost unbroken stream of fast notes beneath them. It ends faster still, in a rush.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 1, cello
mainIdeas.description: a broad, sad melody in long notes, rising and falling, over [[syncopation|syncopated]] piano chords that never settle on the beat.

mainIdeas.name: Theme 2, cello again
mainIdeas.description: a warmer, calmer tune in A major.

mainIdeas.name: The piano’s flood
mainIdeas.description: fast broken chords and runs, the “modern” writing Hiller asked for.

stops.hear: The cello sings a long, dark melody; the piano pulses quietly underneath, off the beat
The violin takes up the melody, the cello weaving a second line around it
stops.happening: The song passes to the violin

stops.hear: The piano breaks into a storm of fast notes; all three play loudly
stops.happening: The music grows towards the second theme

stops.hear: Calm again: the cello sings a warmer, gentler tune
Fragments of the first song pass between the instruments, through darker keys
Violin and cello play a tune together in [[unison|unison]], while the piano ripples beneath in quick broken chords
stops.happening: The brightest moment of the development

stops.hear: The cello’s first song returns
The warm second tune comes back, now in the home key
Faster and more urgent, to a hard ending in D minor

notice: Listen to the piano’s left and right hands in the first minute: they alternate so quickly that the accompaniment seems to shiver. This is what keeps the music agitated while the cello sings slowly.

movements.heading: Andante con moto tranquillo
movements.summary: A song for the piano alone, then for the strings. It sounds like one of Mendelssohn’s *Songs without Words*, his short piano pieces shaped like songs: a melody in the right hand, a gentle accompaniment and a steady bass. The middle section grows darker and more passionate, then the song returns.

mainIdeas.name: The song
mainIdeas.description: a calm, eight-bar melody in B-flat major, first in the piano’s right hand.

mainIdeas.name: The middle
mainIdeas.description: in the minor, more restless, with a falling figure that recalls the first movement.

stops.hear: The piano alone plays a calm, simple melody over a soft accompaniment
stops.happening: The song, like a *Song without Words*

stops.hear: The violin sings the melody, the cello adds a second line below
stops.happening: The strings take over the song

stops.hear: The music turns to the minor and grows restless
The three instruments rise together to the loudest point of the movement
stops.happening: The climax of the middle section

stops.hear: The calm melody returns

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The melody fades over a few quiet chords

notice: Follow the melody as it passes from piano to violin to cello. Mendelssohn never lets one instrument keep it for long.

movements.heading: Scherzo: Leggiero e vivace
movements.summary: A [[scherzo|scherzo]] at top speed, light and quiet almost all the way through. The piano starts alone with a skipping tune; the strings join with short, quick notes, and the three toss the tune between them like a ball.

mainIdeas.name: The skipping tune
mainIdeas.description: fast, light, short notes in groups of three, first in the piano.
A brief singing passage in the middle, which some hear as related to the first movement.

stops.hear: The piano alone, very fast and very quiet, a skipping tune
Violin and cello join with quick, light notes
stops.happening: The tune is tossed between the three

stops.hear: The skipping slows into a short, more singing passage
stops.happening: A lyrical moment in the middle

stops.hear: The skipping tune is back in the piano

stops.label: Near the end
stops.hear: The music thins out and disappears, very softly

notice: Try to tap along: the beat is about one bar per second, and it barely lets up.

movements.heading: Finale: Allegro assai appassionato
movements.summary: A restless, dance-like theme in D minor keeps coming back, in the manner of a [[rondo|rondo]], with contrasting ideas between its returns. The piano part is the busiest in the work. In the middle the cello sings a broad, hopeful new melody, and shortly before the end the music breaks into D major.

mainIdeas.name: The main theme
mainIdeas.description: a nervous, jumping tune in D minor, first heard in the piano.

mainIdeas.name: The cello’s song
mainIdeas.description: a broad, warm melody, marked *cantabile*, that arrives halfway through.

stops.hear: The piano alone plays a nervous, jumping tune
stops.happening: The main theme, in D minor

stops.hear: Violin and cello take up the tune; the piano races
stops.happening: The main theme with all three

stops.hear: A smoother, more flowing idea
The jumping tune again
The cello sings a broad, warm melody, full of hope
stops.happening: A new tune in the middle of the finale

stops.hear: The jumping tune once more, more forceful
The cello’s broad melody comes back, now joined by the violin
The music bursts into D major, faster, to a bright, loud end

notice: Listen for the change of colour near the end, when D minor gives way to D major. The struggle of the whole trio is resolved in a few seconds.

notes.title: In this recording
notes.body: The violinist Itzhak Perlman, the cellist Yo-Yo Ma and the pianist Emanuel Ax recorded both of Mendelssohn’s piano trios in New York in March 2009, two hundred years after the composer’s birth. It was their first recording together as a trio.

threads.title: The singing cello
threads.body: The cello begins the first movement with its long song and brings the hopeful tune of the finale; the violin answers it, and often joins it.

threads.title: The piano in charge
threads.body: After Hiller’s advice the piano part became the heart of the work: it holds the music together, it starts three of the four movements alone, and it rarely stops moving.

threads.title: Songs
threads.body: Mendelssohn’s gift for melody runs through all four movements, from the cello’s first phrase to the *Song without Words* of the Andante.
